title: POC resilience check-in: graceful degradation & rate adjustment

SE to propose conservative retry/backoff config by Tue (Marcus)

summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on recent transient 502/504s and burst-induced rate-limit events. Team validated that a combination of adaptive retries, token-level batching changes, and a short-term routing fallback to smaller model variants reduced tail latency for interactive flows. Action items: share trimmed metrics, run controlled burst tests, and Redwood to propose conservative retry budget and sample configs.
topics: Retry budget and exponential backoff tuning
Graceful degradation: model variants and KV cache priming
Telemetry gaps and log collection for root cause
transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give the first minute to settle, we got a packed agenda. Uh, quick attendance please.

[00:12] Lina Torres: Lina here.

[00:14] Sameer Patel: Sameer on the call.

[00:16] Zoe Kim: Zoe, SRE.

[00:18] Daniel Wu: Daniel product.

[00:20] Marcus Bell: Marcus from Redwood SE. Hey all.

[00:22] Avery Chen: Cool. Alright, so quick recap: last week you saw intermittent 5xxs around mid-day, plus a spike in client-side timeouts. We dug into traces, and it looked like two things: short-lived queueing on the front proxy during bursts, and a small percentage of requests that hit a model variant with a slower cold KV cache. We'll walk through evidence and tuning. Marcus, do you want to start with the latency profile you pulled?

[00:45] Marcus Bell: Yeah sure. So I pulled the trimmed p95/p99 windows from 11/2 to 11/4 — you'll see attached in the sheet but top-level takeaways: during bursts the p99 ballooned from about 560ms to 1.6s, and the runtime 5xxs clustered with these same windows. The proxy returned 502s most times, but there were also 504 timeouts when the client hit their 10s timeout boundary.

[01:10] Sameer Patel: When you say proxy returned 502, is that our gateway or Redwood's edge? We saw 502s in our gateway logs.

[01:16] Marcus Bell: Good question. In about 70% of the cases the return code is observed at your gateway, yes — your gateway was returning the 502 upstream, but trace spans show the request made it to Redwood and the runtime responded with an error code in a small subset. So there's a mix: some are short-lived network flaps between the edge and the runtime, some are legitimate runtime failures.

[01:40] Zoe Kim: Hmm, that matches our snapshots. We also noticed SAML refreshes happening around the same time — maybe a coincidence — but auth re-handshakes created a small surge.

[01:50] Lina Torres: We ran a test yesterday where we sent 150rps for 10 minutes, did you see that in your telemetry?

[01:55] Marcus Bell: Yeah, that's visible. Under that load your average latency stayed fine but we saw the tail widen. Two mitigating items we discussed: adaptive retries with jittered exponential backoff at client side, and a temporary routing fallback to a smaller model variant for interactive requests when we detect sustained latency above threshold.

[02:20] Daniel Wu: About the fallback — what's the cost trade? If we drop to a smaller variant during bursts, will result quality degrade noticeably for our summaries?

[02:28] Marcus Bell: Likely minimal for short completions. For long-context summarization there is some degradation, so we recommended limiting fallback to short interactive endpoints, not long-batch jobs. We can A/B the fallback to measure impact.

[02:45] Sameer Patel: Can you clarify "adaptive retries"? Our current client retries 3x with no jitter — that probably worsens the pile-on during bursts.

[02:52] Marcus Bell: Exactly. Right now zero jitter and tight reattempts cause thundering herd. Proposed: a retry budget of 2 attempts with initial backoff 200ms, exponential factor 2 with full-jitter cap at 2s. Also add a short per-route circuit breaker: if error rate > 10% for 1m, stop retries for 30s for that route and route to the fallback model if enabled.

[03:20] Zoe Kim: If we stop retries, won't we increase user-visible errors?

[03:23] Marcus Bell: Slightly in the short term, but it prevents overload amplification. The idea: better to fail-fast and degrade gracefully than to multiply latency/queueing which causes more 5xxs. Plus you can present a reduced-quality result or a cached prefix while you retry the backend in the background.

[03:42] Lina Torres: You mentioned cached prefix — is that the KV cache you talked about before? We've seen cold-start issues there.

[03:48] Marcus Bell: Yes. KV cache priming matters. If a request routes to an instance without the needed KV warm, the first few tokens are slower. Our runtime supports proactive priming — when we detect a pattern of repeated prompts we can pre-load common prefixes into KV on warm instances. For POC we can pre-warm the top 20 prompts.

[04:05] Sameer Patel: Ok, that's helpful. What's the operational overhead for priming?

[04:09] Marcus Bell: Minimal; it's a background job and we avoid duplication with a token-aware cache key. There's a small memory cost per instance but it's negligible at POC scale.

[04:18] Avery Chen: Quick note — we did see one runtime-level exception traced to a tokenization edge-case in model-v2-2026q3, which Marcus's team is following up on. That accounted for roughly 5% of internal 5xxs in the window. Marcus, can you give status?

[04:34] Marcus Bell: Sure. We've opened issue INF-2398, engineering is shipping a patch that guards the tokenizer and returns a deterministic error rather than a crash. It'll be deployed to canary tonight and we'll watch the metric. That should reduce the internal 5xx class.

[04:50] Daniel Wu: Good. On rate-limits — we saw bursts hitting the token quota mid-day even though request count was modest, because some requests are long. Any short term levers?

[04:58] Marcus Bell: Two levers: 1) token-aware rate limiting at the gateway so you don't get surprised by a few heavy requests consuming quota, and 2) response truncation with a continuation token pattern for long requests so we split user-facing latency across smaller calls. For POC, token-aware windowing is easiest: treat tokens as the unit and give a soft cap that throttle 429s only if sustained.

[05:25] Zoe Kim: Are 429s better than 502s for us? We saw both.

[05:29] Marcus Bell: From an observability and retry perspective, 429 is preferable — it's an explicit client throttle. The clients can backoff and honor the Retry-After. With 502/504 you don't always know if the backend processed the request.

[05:42] Lina Torres: Ok, what about telemetry gaps — we noticed missing spans in certain traces.

[05:46] Marcus Bell: That was probably sampling and a misconfigured agent on your gateway — some spans were dropped at 10% sampling. We recommend bumping sampling to 50% during the next test window. Also include the request_id header from Redwood so we can join traces end-to-end.

[06:05] Sameer Patel: We'll enable higher sampling for the burst tests.

[06:09] Marcus Bell: Great. I've got a suggested runbook for the immediate triage: 1) run two canonical traffic profiles (steady 50rps for 30m, burst 200rps for 30m) with sampling 50%, 2) collect gateway and runtime logs with request_id correlation, 3) apply conservative retry policy and token-aware limits on your gateway, 4) enable fallback to smaller model for interactive routes.

[06:32] Avery Chen: I'll attach the trimmed CSV and the visualized p99 graphs after the call. Link will be in follow-up.

[06:37] Daniel Wu: On SLA implications — if we route to fallback more frequently, do we need to adjust our SLOs?

[06:43] Marcus Bell: Probably yes. The product-level SLO should be based on user experience rather than underlying model. For example set a 95th latency SLO for the interactive path; fallback is allowed if quality metrics remain above threshold. We can help craft an SLO proposal.

[06:58] Zoe Kim: One more operational question: if we do circuit breaker for a route, how do we surface that in dashboards? We don't want silent degradations.

[07:05] Marcus Bell: We push events to the console: circuit state changes, error budget burn, fallback activation, and per-route rate-limit events. We'll also add an alert if a route's fallback is active for more than N minutes.

[07:18] Lina Torres: Perfect. Anything else from Redwood side?

[07:22] Avery Chen: A couple quick clarifications — first, the sample retry config (we'll paste in the follow-up) is intentionally conservative for POC. Second, we recommend running the burst tests during a maintenance window to avoid affecting prod users.

[07:36] Sameer Patel: We'll schedule that for Friday window.

[07:39] Marcus Bell: Also note: we saw a small percentage of 5xxs tied to a specific region failover where a node had an old kernel. That was an ops issue and we rolled a hotfix last week. It's unlikely to reoccur but still worth noting.

[08:00] Daniel Wu: Good. Okay, recap and owners?

[08:03] Avery Chen: Recap — Redwood to share trimmed metrics CSV and graphs (Avery). Marcus to propose retry/backoff and circuit-breaker parameters plus sample client code (Marcus). Customer to run two traffic profiles and collect logs and increase trace sampling (Sameer and Zoe). We also recommended enabling token-aware rate limiting and short-model fallback for interactive endpoints.

[08:25] Lina Torres: Thanks, that matches our notes.

[08:28] Zoe Kim: We'll get logs uploaded and confirm scheduling for Friday.

[08:31] Avery Chen: Great. I'll send meeting notes and attach the artifacts — request_latencies_2026-11-02_to_11-05.csv and a short runbook. Also sending the link to the shared metrics sheet: https://redwood.app/sheets/poc-metrics-54712 (internal).

[08:46] Daniel Wu: Thanks everyone.

[08:48] Marcus Bell: Thanks.

[08:50] Meeting ends.

Notes on transcription: occasional cross-talk and truncated words. Proper nouns like "KV cache" sometimes transcribed as "K V cache" and product variant names may be slightly off (model-v2 vs model-v2-2026q3).
